title: Do You Know What Hurts Me?
text:
Rabbi Moshe Leib of Sasov was a Hasidic master known for his tireless love of ordinary people. He used to say that he had learned what it means to love from a peasant.

He had stopped at a country inn, where two peasants were sitting at a table, drinking. They had both had a fair amount, and they were in the warm and sentimental mood that drink can bring.

One of them turned to the other. "Tell me," he said, "do you love me?"

"Of course I love you," said the other. "I love you very much."

The first man shook his head. "You say you love me," he said, "but you do not know what hurts me. If you really loved me, you would know."

The second man had no answer to that, and the two of them sat on in silence. But the rabbi, according to the story, understood. To love people, he concluded, is to know their needs and to bear the burden of their sorrow.
lesson: Saying you care is easy. Showing it means paying enough attention to know what hurts the people you love, and acting on that knowledge.
people: Rabbi Moshe Leib of Sasov, two peasants
source: Hasidic tradition, retold in Martin Buber, Tales of the Hasidim
